framework.name: NIST SP 800-53
framework.summary: The US federal catalogue of security and privacy controls from NIST. Federal agencies and many government contractors must use it, and FedRAMP builds on it for cloud services. US auditors often ask for it. This is the Moderate baseline: 177 base controls in 18 families.

requirements.title: Written rules and procedures for access control are approved, shared and kept current.
Accounts are requested, approved, reviewed and removed under one managed process.
Systems enforce the approved access rights before anyone reaches information or functions.
Information moves within and between systems only along approved paths.
Duties are split so no single person can misuse a system unchecked.
People and processes get only the access their tasks require.
Repeated failed sign-in attempts lead to a lockout or a delay.
Users see a notice about permitted use and monitoring before signing in.
Idle devices lock the screen and need sign-in again to continue.
User sessions end automatically after set conditions such as long inactivity.
Any action allowed without signing in is listed, justified and kept minimal.
Each kind of remote access has its own rules and is approved first.
Wireless access is restricted, configured securely and approved before use.
Mobile devices connect to company systems only under set conditions.
Rules say when outside systems may be used to work with company information.
Users can check that a partner may see information before sharing it.
Only approved people publish content, and it is checked for non-public information.
Training and awareness rules and procedures are written down and kept current.
Everyone gets security and privacy awareness training on joining and regularly afterwards.
People with security or privacy duties are trained for their particular role.
Records show who completed which security training and when.
Rules and procedures for audit logging are approved, shared and reviewed regularly.
The organisation decides which events its systems must log, and reviews that choice.
Each log entry says what happened, when, where, from what source and to whom.
Enough storage is set aside so logs are not lost when space runs out.
Someone is alerted and acts when logging stops working.
Logs are reviewed for signs of misuse, and findings reach the right people.
Tools can filter and summarise logs to support investigations and reports.
Log entries carry accurate time stamps from the system clock, mappable to UTC.
Logs and logging tools are protected from tampering and unauthorised access.
Logs are kept long enough to support investigations and legal duties.
Systems actually record the chosen events, with the components and settings defined.
Rules and procedures for assessing and authorising systems are written and kept current.
Controls are assessed regularly against an approved plan, and the results are reported to those accountable.
Information exchanged with other systems is covered by an agreement on security duties.
Known weaknesses are tracked in a plan with owners, actions and dates.
A senior official accepts the remaining risk before a system goes into operation.
Controls and risks are monitored continuously against a defined strategy.
Internal connections between system components are approved and their purpose recorded.
Configuration management rules and procedures are written down and kept up to date.
Each system has a documented, approved baseline configuration that is kept current.
Changes to systems are proposed, reviewed, approved, recorded and checked afterwards.
The security and privacy effect of a change is assessed before it is made.
Only approved people can make changes to systems, physically or logically.
Secure settings are defined for every component, applied and deviations recorded.
Systems run only the functions, ports and services they actually need.
An accurate inventory lists every system component with enough detail to track it.
A configuration management plan sets roles, processes and what falls under it.
Software and documentation are used only as their licences and contracts allow.
Rules decide what software users may install, and the rules are enforced.
The organisation knows where its information is held and processed.
Contingency planning rules and procedures are approved, shared and reviewed regularly.
A contingency plan says how essential functions continue and systems are restored.
People with contingency roles are trained for them and refreshed regularly.
The contingency plan is tested, and the results lead to corrections.
Backups are stored at a separate site that can be reached when needed.
An alternate site can take over essential processing within agreed times.
Backup communication links can carry essential services if the main ones fail.
User, system and documentation backups are made regularly and kept safe.
Systems can be recovered to a known secure state after a disruption.
Identification and sign-in rules and procedures are written down and kept current.
Every staff user is uniquely identified and proves who they are at sign-in.
Devices are identified and authenticated before they may connect.
User and device identifiers are assigned with approval and never reused too soon.
Passwords, keys and other authenticators are issued, protected and changed safely.
Sign-in screens hide what is typed so onlookers cannot read secrets.
Access to cryptographic modules requires authentication that meets the applicable standards.
Users from outside the organisation are also uniquely identified and authenticated.
Users must sign in again in set situations, such as changing roles.
People's identities are verified with evidence before they receive accounts.
Incident response rules and procedures are approved, shared and reviewed regularly.
People with incident roles are trained for them on joining and regularly afterwards.
The ability to respond to incidents is tested regularly.
Incidents are handled from preparation and detection through containment to recovery.
Every incident is tracked and documented from start to finish.
Suspected incidents are reported quickly inside the organisation and to the authorities.
Users can turn to a support resource for help with incidents.
An approved incident response plan sets out roles, steps and reporting.
Rules and procedures for system maintenance are written down and kept current.
Maintenance is scheduled, approved, recorded and checked once the work is done.
Tools used for maintenance are approved, controlled, monitored and reviewed.
Remote maintenance is approved, strongly authenticated, logged and closed when finished.
Only authorised people carry out maintenance, and others are supervised.
Support and spare parts for key components are available within agreed times.
Rules and procedures for protecting storage media are approved and reviewed regularly.
Only authorised people can get at digital and paper media.
Media are labelled with how they may be handled and shared.
Media are stored securely until they are destroyed or wiped.
Media taken outside secure areas are protected and tracked on the way.
Media are wiped or destroyed before disposal or reuse.
Certain kinds of media are restricted or banned on company systems.
Physical and environmental protection rules and procedures are written down and kept current.
A current list shows who may enter the facility, reviewed regularly.
Entry and exit points are controlled so only authorised people get in.
Cabling and network lines inside the facility are protected from tampering.
Printers, screens and other output devices are placed where outsiders cannot read them.
Physical access is monitored so incidents are detected and answered.
Records of visitors are kept and reviewed for a set period.
Power equipment and cables for systems are protected from damage.
Power to systems can be cut quickly in an emergency, safely and securely.
Backup power lets systems shut down cleanly or keep running when mains fail.
Automatic emergency lighting works when the power goes out and covers exits.
Fire detection and suppression systems protect the facility and are maintained.
Temperature and humidity in equipment rooms stay within safe limits and are monitored.
Shutoff valves and other measures protect systems from water leaks.
Equipment entering and leaving the facility is authorised, controlled and recorded.
Staff working at other sites follow set security controls there.
Security planning rules and procedures are approved, shared and reviewed regularly.
Each system has an approved plan describing its boundary, risks and controls.
Users sign agreed rules on how they must behave with systems and information.
Security and privacy architectures describe how systems protect information by design.
A control baseline is chosen that fits the system and its risks.
The chosen control baseline is adjusted to fit the organisation and the system.
Personnel security rules and procedures are written down, shared and kept current.
Each position is rated by risk, and the rating guides screening.
People are screened before they get access, and again when required.
When people leave, their access ends and company property is recovered.
When people move roles, their access is reviewed and adjusted promptly.
People sign access and confidentiality agreements before they are given access.
External staff must meet set security requirements, and compliance is monitored.
A formal sanctions process applies to people who break security rules.
Job descriptions state the security and privacy duties of each role.
Risk assessment rules and procedures are approved, shared and reviewed regularly.
Systems and information are rated by the harm a loss would cause.
Risks to systems and information are assessed, recorded and updated regularly.
Systems are scanned for vulnerabilities regularly and the findings are fixed.
Findings from assessments and monitoring are answered according to the risk tolerance.
The components and functions most critical to the mission are identified.
Rules and procedures for acquiring systems and services are written and kept current.
Security and privacy needs are budgeted for when planning systems.
Systems are built and run under a life cycle that includes security.
Contracts for systems and services state the security and privacy requirements.
Administrator and user documentation for each system is obtained and kept available.
Systems are designed and changed following sound security and privacy engineering principles.
External service providers must meet set security requirements and are monitored.
Developers control and track changes to the systems they build.
Developers test their systems for security flaws and fix what they find.
Developers follow a defined process with set standards and tools.
Components no longer supported by their maker are replaced or specially justified.
Rules and procedures for protecting systems and communications are written and kept current.
User functions are kept apart from system administration functions.
Shared system resources do not leak information from one user to another.
Systems withstand or limit the effects of denial-of-service attacks.
Traffic at external and key internal boundaries is monitored and controlled.
Information is protected against reading or changing while it is transmitted.
Network connections end after a session closes or stays inactive too long.
Cryptographic keys are created, distributed, stored and destroyed under set rules.
Encryption uses the types required by law, policy and the risk.
Cameras and microphones cannot be switched on remotely, and users see when active.
Public key certificates are issued under an approved policy or from approved providers.
Code that runs inside documents or web pages is allowed only under set rules.
Authoritative DNS answers are signed so others can verify where they came from.
Resolvers check the origin and integrity of the DNS answers they receive.
DNS services are built redundantly and kept apart for internal and external use.
Communication sessions are protected against hijacking and forged messages.
Stored information is protected against unauthorised reading or change.
Each process runs in its own execution space, kept apart from others.
Rules and procedures for system and information integrity are written and kept current.
Flaws are found, reported and fixed, with updates tested and installed promptly.
Malicious code is detected and blocked at entry points and on systems.
Systems are monitored to detect attacks, unauthorised use and unusual activity.
Security alerts and advisories from outside are received, shared and acted upon.
Integrity checks detect unauthorised changes to software, firmware and information.
Spam is detected and blocked where email and other messages enter.
Systems check that the information they receive is valid before using it.
Error messages help users without revealing information attackers could exploit.
Information is managed and kept only as long as law and policy require.
Memory protections stop code from running where it should not.
Supply chain risk rules and procedures are written down, shared and kept current.
A plan sets out how supply chain risks are identified and managed.
Processes and controls protect against supply chain risks to systems and components.
Purchasing methods are chosen to reduce supply chain risks.
Suppliers and the services they provide are assessed and reviewed regularly.
Suppliers agree to report compromises and other supply chain events promptly.
Systems and components are inspected for signs of tampering.
Counterfeit components are prevented, detected and reported.
Components and data are disposed of securely at the end of their use.
